content: Halo nevus, also known as leukoderma acquisitum centrifugum, perinevoid vitiligo, or Sutton nevus, is a type of mole characterized by a surrounding depigmented ring, often referred to as a halo. The pathophysiology of halo nevus involves an autoimmune process in which CD8+ T lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, target and destroy melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells in the skin. The exact trigger for this immune response remains unknown. Epidemiologically, halo nevi are observed in approximately 1% of the general population. They occur equally across all races and sexes, although there is evidence of a familial predisposition. The condition most commonly manifests during adolescence. Certain risk factors are associated with the development of halo nevi. These include a personal or family history of vitiligo, malignant melanoma, or Turner syndrome. On physical examination, a halo nevus is identified as a mole (nevus) surrounded by a distinct area of depigmentation, giving it the appearance of a halo. This characteristic presentation is well-documented in dermatological literature and atlases. The natural history of halo nevi is generally benign. In some cases, the depigmented area may spontaneously regain pigment over time. While halo nevi are not harmful, it is crucial to monitor them regularly. Any changes in the appearance of existing lesions or the development of new ones should be carefully noted. If a halo nevus becomes painful, itchy, or shows signs of infection, medical evaluation is necessary to rule out the possibility of melanoma. Treatment for halo nevi is typically unnecessary, as the condition is of cosmetic concern only. Patients with halo nevi are usually asymptomatic and do not require medical intervention.
